vignette:
He is a 34-year-old South Eastern Asian man who comes across as careful with his words, as if each one has to pass through a gate before he can say it aloud. He works as a chaplain, and his presence with other people is usually calm and attentive, but what becomes clear over several sessions is how much effort it takes for him to keep that calm in place. He is widowed, and the loss of his spouse sits in the background of his life like a grief he has learned to carry in public, even while another fear has taken hold of him more recently.

The robbery happens on an ordinary evening, on a stretch of street he has used many times without thinking. He is leaving a pharmacy after buying supplies for work, carrying a folder of notes and a small bag, when two men step toward him too quickly for him to understand what is happening. One blocks his path, the other comes from the side. He remembers the smell of damp concrete, the hard shine of a passing car’s headlights, and the absurdity of noticing the bruise-colored sky while his body is already bracing for impact. One of them demands his wallet and phone. When he hesitates, trying to reason with them, they shove him, and he falls hard enough to crack his elbow against the pavement. He gives them what they want, but the fear does not end when they run. It stays in his chest, in the ringing in his ears, in the sudden knowledge that the world can turn predatory without warning.

In the days afterward, he tells himself he is lucky. He was not stabbed. He was not left unconscious. He repeats these facts the way other people might recite a prayer. But his body does not accept the reassurance. He starts scanning every street before he steps onto it, turning his head at footsteps behind him, gripping his keys so tightly they leave marks in his palm. The route to the pharmacy becomes impossible to take again. He begins driving even short distances because walking feels too exposed. At night, he wakes with his heart pounding, certain for a moment that someone is outside the bedroom door. His wife used to be the one who could settle him when he was troubled; since her death, the apartment already feels too quiet, and now the silence has sharpened into something he listens to with dread.

At work, he still shows up. That matters to him. As a chaplain, people come to him in hospitals, homes, and places of grief, expecting steadiness. He stands with families at bedsides, bows his head in prayer, and listens to stories of loss with the same gentle attention he has always offered. But he notices that his own mind is frequently elsewhere. When a patient raises their voice, he flinches. If someone approaches him from behind in a hallway, his whole body tightens before he can stop it. He starts choosing chairs with his back to the wall. He avoids dark parking lots and refuses evening visits when he can, saying he has another obligation. He does not tell colleagues why. He worries that if he speaks about the robbery, he will seem weak or unable to do the job he has always considered a calling.

The memories come back without invitation, especially in moments that should be ordinary. The squeal of brakes can send him back to the street. The smell of wet pavement after rain can make his stomach drop. He sees the men’s faces in fragments, never clearly, but enough to feel the same helplessness returning. Sometimes he feels the impact of falling before he remembers he is indoors. Other times he is filled with a hot, helpless anger at himself for not fighting, for freezing, for handing over his belongings so quickly. He knows rationally that compliance may have saved him, yet shame keeps circling back.

He becomes more withdrawn, though people around him may only notice that he is more tired, less available, slower to answer messages. He eats without appetite. He starts checking locks multiple times at night, and if he hears voices outside the building, he stands still until he is sure they are moving away. He avoids talking about his wife as well, because the robbery has made his grief feel more exposed, as if everything he has lost is now part of the same vulnerable map of his life.

Still, he continues to come in each week, dressed neatly, speaking softly, trying to make sense of how faith, duty, mourning, and fear now coexist in him. He wants to believe he can return to the man who moved through the world with trust, but for now he lives by anticipation, by caution, by the constant effort of keeping his body from remembering what it already knows.
